2611.02341.tldr: An MLLM agent plans a world state and metric camera trajectories with structured prompts, while an autoregressive camera-controlled video model stores generated chunks with geometry in a point-cloud memory. Occlusion-aware history selection and reliability-based memory maintenance give SOTA on revisiting and exploration benchmarks.
2611.02341.why: Directly relevant to video world models with 3D-consistent long-horizon generation, geometry-based spatial memory, and camera control (PRoPE). Memory retrieval and maintenance ideas may transfer to your work.
2611.02341.reason: Video world model with spatial memory and geometry for persistent exploration
2611.02341.qn: Sensible system combining agent and geometric memory; novelty is mostly incremental engineering.
2611.02341.abs: Recent interactive video world models generate visually compelling videos from a single image, following user-provided camera motion and text prompts. However, such low-level control demands substantial user effort to realize a high-level intent, and the generated world struggles to remain persistent as the exploration proceeds. In this work, we present AgiWorld, an agentic video world model that explores and builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction. For high-level planning, our agent AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey through it in a world state and directs the exploration. For low-level realization, our video world model AgiWorld-WM generates the video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in a spatial memory, from which the agent updates its world state. This closed loop keeps the world faithful to the user's intent and keeps the agent's world state consistent with the generated content throughout the exploration. We co-design the two levels around the shared spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. In AgiWorld-WM, to handle occlusion and accumulated geometric errors in the spatial memory over long rollouts, we propose occlusion-aware history selection, which retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance, which prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations. AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks, and qualitative results and ablations show that AgiWorld builds persistent worlds from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys. Persistence thus arises not from the video model alone but from its closed loop with the agent.

2611.01648.tldr: Adds a writer-specific LoRA residual for KV written to the cache of causal video generators, and trains it via a differentiable paged KV cache with local rematerialization; gains VBench-Long aesthetic quality of 6.6 to 8.5 points over Self Gradient Forcing, with 28% less memory.
2611.01648.why: Relevant to autoregressive video world models and long-horizon consistency; the differentiable KV cache training trick and separate memory representations could transfer to your efficient causal video diffusion work.
2611.01648.reason: Differentiable KV cache for causal video generators; directly on video diffusion efficiency
2611.01648.qn: Clever systems and memory idea, but evidence is VBench-centric and builds on a narrow baseline lineage.
2611.01648.abs: A causal video generator produces two key--value (KV) states for every segment: the KV it uses while denoising that segment, and the KV it writes into the cache for later segments to read. In a pretrained generator the two already differ substantially, later segments attend to them differently, and replacing the written KV with the generation KV degrades the continuation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV) to learn a dedicated memory representation from its future use: a writer-specific low-rank residual on the shared backbone separates memory writing from generation and is trained through the future reads of what it writes. Learning a write from its future use needs gradients through the cache, which the mutable cache in common use cannot provide. dKV Forcing replaces the training-time cache by persistent differentiable pages with local rematerialization and, in one temporal traversal, computes exactly the gradient that a two-pass reconstruction of the same objective computes. One traversal computes the full memory gradient at $7\%$ generator-update overhead over detached-write training, with $28\%$ less resident memory and $20.8\%$ shorter training cycles than the two-pass reconstruction. Over Self Gradient Forcing (SGF), the same objective trained with the same traversal, writer adaptation raises VBench-Long aesthetic quality by $6.6$ points at 60\,s and $8.5$ points at 240\,s with the highest subject and background consistency, and rollout dropout of the residual keeps most of this gain while restoring the motion of training without write gradients.

2611.01543.tldr: GSExplorer loops a video generator conditioned on renderings (RGB, depth, opacity, holes) from a persistent 3DGS scene with SLAM-based reconstruction, inconsistency filtering and cross-chunk bundle adjustment; reports best WorldScore results and strong 481-frame revisit consistency.
2611.01543.why: Directly relevant to 3D-consistent video world models with camera control; combines 3DGS memory, video diffusion and SLAM reconstruction for long-horizon exploration.
2611.01543.reason: Persistent 3DGS world state with video generation and camera control
2611.01543.qn: Sensible system integration, but novelty is incremental and evidence appears limited to few benchmarks.
2611.01543.abs: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging as target-view guidance becomes incomplete and inconsistencies accumulate across repeated scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a condition-driven video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos are then fed back to a SLAM-based reconstruction backend, where inconsistency filtering prevents conflicting content from corrupting the scene and cross-chunk bundle adjustment improves spatial alignment across generation steps. We further design a data-construction pipeline that reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation, yielding 293K training pairs of degraded multimodal renderings and real target videos. GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on both single-step and three-step WorldScore evaluation, with strong camera control and consistency across both settings, including a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation. On 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts, it also shows strong revisit consistency, demonstrating the value of maintaining a reliable 3D world state for continued exploration.

2611.04764.tldr: U-JiT is a UNet-like transformer that varies patch size with depth (down to single pixels) with skip connections, enabling pixel-space video flow matching; on Kinetics-600 it improves FVD by 27% over prior SOTA and beats latent baselines at high compression.
2611.04764.why: Pixel-space video diffusion transformers remove the VAE and offer an alternative to latent video models; the hierarchical-patch design and efficient attention are relevant to efficient video DiT work.
2611.04764.reason: Pixel-space video diffusion architecture; strongly relevant to video generation
2611.04764.qn: Controlled from-scratch comparisons on Kinetics-600, but small scale and a single dataset.
2611.04764.abs: Latent diffusion and flow matching models are ubiquitous in state-of-the-art generative video models. While highly effective, relying on pretrained autoencoders to compress the data into a lower-dimensional latent space also comes with drawbacks. First, training proceeds in two stages: autoencoder pretraining, with compression and reconstruction objectives, followed by latent generative model training, precluding fully end-to-end training. Second, autoencoders also lead to an inherent loss of signal, and the trade-off between reconstruction quality and generative performance in the latent space is still an active area of research. In this paper we explore the viability of generative video models directly in pixel space. We analyze recent approaches in pixel-space generative modeling of images that rely on basic transformer designs, and identify several shortcomings that limit their effectiveness for the high-dimensional pixel-space video generation. To overcome these limitations, we propose a UNet-like transformer architecture along with improvements to the training recipe and sampling strategy. We conduct controlled experiments, training latent and pixel-space models from scratch on Kinetics-600. For the standard frames-to-video task at 128 resolution, our U-JiT model improves generative FVD by 27% over prior state-of-the-art results, and by 14% against the JiT pixel-space baseline. Scaling to higher 256 resolution, we find the improvement over pixel-space and latent-based models grows as we increase the spatiotemporal compression rate up to $64 \times 64 \times 8$. Finally, we find that U-JiT improves per-frame FID by 27% over latent models and 61% over pixel-space models on class-to-video generation, with respectively 9% and 56% reduction in FVD.

2611.04028.tldr: Proposes Compression Forcing: a learned tokenizer (DAT) orders history tokens by dynamics saliency, a diffusion world model conditions on variable-length prefixes, and guidance mixes full and prefix-conditioned scores. Reports gains in video forecasting, games, robotics, and policy evaluation.
2611.04028.why: Relevant to video world models and history conditioning in diffusion transformers; ordered, nested tokens for memory compression and guidance could carry over to long-context, camera-controlled video generation.
2611.04028.reason: History compression for diffusion world models, close to world model interests
2611.04028.qn: Interesting principle and broad environments; unclear baseline strength and ablations from the intro alone.
2611.04028.abs: Effective world modeling requires compressing salient history information that facilitates future prediction. However, most existing approaches inherit tokenization and conditioning mechanisms from video generation, where objectives are centered around perceptual realism rather than predictive utility. This discrepancy limits the world model's effectiveness, especially in environments dominated by visual nuisances or task-irrelevant background details. To this end, we introduce Compression Forcing (CF), a general framework that aligns history compression with the predictive objective of world modeling. Compression Forcing features Dynamics-Aware Tokenization (DAT), a novel tokenization method that compresses history observations into a sequence ordered by decreasing dynamics saliency. Built on a diffusion backbone, this structure enables Hierarchical History Guidance (HG-H), allowing selective amplification of dynamics-salient information during inference. Extensive experiments across various environments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity, physical realism, and downstream decision-making performance, establishing Compression Forcing as a highly flexible and effective approach for world modeling.

2611.00758.tldr: ReDate is a training-free method for memory in interactive video world models. It re-dates retrieved tokens by valid time from the action log, so reverted regions are shown correctly. It raises FAR's current-state share after undo from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19.
2611.00758.why: It addresses memory consistency in camera-controlled video world models, and shows that timestamp or RoPE positions act as a latest-wins rule that can be repurposed without retraining.
2611.00758.reason: Memory for interactive video world models with undo handling; directly relevant
2611.00758.qn: Clever training-free fix with theory, but narrow setting and relies on action logs.
2611.00758.abs: Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.

2611.01627.tldr: EgoMo3R jointly optimizes camera poses, scene geometry, and full-body motion from monocular egocentric video, combining monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks with a diffusion motion prior via alternating optimization; it beats specialized baselines on EgoExo4D and Nymeria.
2611.01627.why: Relevant as an optimization-based 4D reconstruction approach that pairs feed-forward geometric primitives with a diffusion prior to get metric, gravity-aligned scenes in dynamic video.
2611.01627.reason: Joint egocentric motion and scene reconstruction; touches 3D reconstruction and motion priors
2611.01627.qn: Sensible joint-optimization design with good insights; pipeline is mostly composed of existing components.
2611.01627.abs: Understanding holistic 3D human motion and the surrounding environment from egocentric video is fundamental for applications in AR/VR and robotics. Although these tasks are inherently coupled, existing methods treat them separately. In particular, egocentric motion reconstruction methods typically assume access to metric, gravity-aligned camera trajectories from specialized inertial sensors. Recovering such trajectories from monocular egocentric video remains a significant challenge due to rapid head movements and motion blur. We present EgoMo3R, a joint optimization framework that simultaneously reconstructs 3D human motion and scene geometry from casual egocentric video. It leverages the robustness of low-level visuo-geometric primitives, including monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks, integrated with a diffusion-based human motion prior via first-order optimization. We propose an alternating optimization scheme that establishes a synergistic feedback loop: scene reconstruction provides physical grounding and trajectory conditioning for the motion prior, while the motion prior regularizes the camera trajectory and anchors the scene in a metric, gravity-aligned world frame. We evaluate EgoMo3R on the highly dynamic sequences of the EgoExo4D and Nymeria datasets and show that it outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.

2611.01677.tldr: Technical report on a streaming causal multi-view world model for driving and robotics, combining view-temporal attention with multi-view RoPE, gated linear attention in temporal layers, feed-forward 4D Gaussian renderings (WorldRec 2.0) as scene memory, and distillation.
2611.01677.why: It combines your interests: feed-forward static/dynamic Gaussian reconstruction as conditioning, multi-view video DiT with RoPE, GLA for efficient streaming, and distillation for closed-loop use.
2611.01677.reason: Causal world model with 3D Gaussians, multi-view RoPE, linear attention; closely matches interests
2611.01677.qn: System-style report with many components; no ablations or baselines visible in the introduction.
2611.01677.abs: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.

2611.05377.tldr: DreamX repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer as a latent action learner, using learnable query tokens to compress 1,200 frame tokens into 4 latent action tokens. It reports SOTA among latent action models on LARY-Bench and shows cross-embodiment video and action transfer.
2611.05377.why: It uses video DiT features and a generative prior for controllable dynamics, and the compact latent actions could lower the cost of video-diffusion policies and world models.
2611.05377.reason: Uses video diffusion model features for latent actions; adjacent to video world models
2611.05377.qn: Sensible idea with SOTA claims, but the intro gives limited ablation or baseline detail.
2611.05377.abs: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.

2611.03992.tldr: FlagRot picks, per 32-channel key sub-vector, whether to store it Hadamard-rotated or plain based on calibrated attention error, with the choice stored in the scale sign bit. At 2.5 bits it cuts KIVI's KL from 18.7 to 12.4 ×10^-3 and gains up to +2.9 on RULER at 128k.
2611.03992.why: KV cache quantization is a key lever for efficient long-context transformer inference. The finding that rotation hurts flat sub-vectors may carry over to quantizing video DiT activations and KV caches.
2611.03992.reason: Low-bit KV cache quantization; relates to efficient transformer inference.
2611.03992.qn: Sound, practical observation with vLLM integration; gains modest and calibration-dependent.
2611.03992.abs: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.

2611.01320.tldr: Training-free sparse attention for diffusion LLMs: refreshes block-sparse masks at anchor denoising steps, reuses them within locally stable intervals, and gives heads adaptive budgets. Gets 2.78x speedup over FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 90% sparsity.
2611.01320.why: Sparse attention with step-wise mask reuse across denoising steps and head-adaptive budgets maps directly onto efficient video diffusion transformer inference; the same temporal-stationarity idea may transfer.
2611.01320.reason: Sparse attention and caching for diffusion LLMs; relevant efficiency technique
2611.01320.qn: Sensible, well-motivated incremental improvement over SparseD; evidence limited to two dLLMs.
2611.01320.abs: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

2611.00027.tldr: Scale-Free Attention keeps exact local attention and summarizes distant blocks by mean-pooled keys and values with a log block-size logit correction under one shared softmax, giving O(N log N) cost. It reports a 357× speedup over FlashAttention at 262k tokens and FID 12.51 vs 13.25 for full attention.
2611.00027.why: Directly relevant to efficient and sparse attention for diffusion transformers. It is a drop-in, parameter-free replacement that can be fine-tuned from full-attention checkpoints, and may extend to video DiTs with very long token sequences.
2611.00027.reason: Efficient attention for diffusion transformers; relevant to inference efficiency interests
2611.00027.qn: Simple, principled design with a drop-in claim; evidence is limited to small-scale training and short fine-tunes.
2611.00027.abs: Diffusion transformers have achieved remarkable success in image generation, but accelerating attention while preserving generation quality remains a major challenge at high resolutions. Inspired by statistical physics and the widespread occurrence of scale-free laws in nature, we introduce Scale-Free Attention (SFA), which preserves fine local interactions while summarizing distant regions at progressively coarser scales. For $N$ tokens, mean pooling, token-count correction, and a shared softmax over a scale-free spatial hierarchy give SFA $O(N\log N)$ complexity in both forward and backward passes. Our Triton implementation achieves $357.3\times$ forward and $265.6\times$ backward attention speedups over FlashAttention at 262,144 tokens. After 40 epochs of PixelFlow training from scratch on ImageNet at $256\times256$ resolution, SFA achieves the best generation quality among five attention mechanisms, including full attention. Fr\'echet inception distance evaluated on 50,000 generated samples (FID-50k) improves from 13.25 for full attention to 12.51, and the advantage over full attention persists through 80 epochs. SFA also achieves the best generation quality among the compared efficient-attention methods on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ). Beyond training from scratch, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with attention replaced by SFA retains the generation quality of its full-attention counterpart under matched fine-tuning budgets. We obtain similar results when fine-tuning pretrained PixelFlow on ImageNet. SFA establishes scale-free structure as an effective design principle for efficient, high-quality diffusion transformers.

2611.02508.tldr: AttentionIndex replaces exhaustive indexer scoring in learned sparse attention (DSA) with a causal, incrementally maintained inverted-file index. At 1M tokens it gives 1.3-1.8x prefill throughput over exhaustive selection and 10-17 points higher top-k recall than HiSA at similar speed.
2611.02508.why: Sparse attention selection is an efficiency bottleneck for long-context transformers; the IVF-style routing idea could transfer to long-video DiT sparse attention, though this paper targets LLM prefill.
2611.02508.reason: Efficient sparse attention selection for LLMs; transferable ideas, though not video diffusion
2611.02508.qn: Solid systems work on production models; LLM-only, with a narrow baseline set.
2611.02508.abs: Learned sparse attention, used in production models such as DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5, lets each query attend to only k keys chosen by a lightweight indexer, but the indexer still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, this selection takes more than half of prefill time. Two-stage selection over contiguous blocks, as in HiSA, reduces this cost, but its recall declines as context grows at a fixed candidate budget. We present AttentionIndex, which routes each query over an inverted-file index that groups indexer keys by similarity and refines the candidates with the native indexer score. AttentionIndex builds the index during prefill, making new keys searchable immediately, reusing previous clustering to keep maintenance cheap, and exposing each query only to clusters built from its own prefix. On GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at one million tokens, AttentionIndex delivers 1.3-1.8 times the prefill throughput of exhaustive selection, and at throughput within 5% of HiSA, it recovers 17.0 and 10.0 percentage points more of the exhaustive top-k, respectively. AttentionIndex also improves accuracy on long-context benchmarks by up to 18.4 percentage points over HiSA at the same candidate budget.

2611.04666.tldr: Phase-DGS replaces frame timestamps with a learned semantic phase of the motion cycle, so unsynchronized multi-view videos train 4D Gaussian Splatting coherently; reports up to +8.5 dB PSNR over baselines under offsets, drops, and freezes.
2611.04666.why: Directly relevant to 4D reconstruction from real captures; a plug-and-play module for RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS addresses a practical synchronization failure in dynamic GS.
2611.04666.reason: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting from unsynchronized cameras; relevant to 4D reconstruction
2611.04666.qn: Neat plug-in idea; likely limited to periodic or repeated motion, with unclear generality.
2611.04666.abs: Spatiotemporal scene reconstruction with Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS) fundamentally depends on perfect temporal synchronization across all cameras, an assumption rarely achievable in practice. Industry-standard synchronization requires expensive specialized hardware and complex setup, while data-driven alternatives including audio-based alignment, geometry matching, and pose tracking remain limited by restrictive environmental or scene-specific assumptions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Phase-DGS, a framework that replaces conventional timestamps with a semantic phase representing each frame's inherent state within the underlying motion cycle. Frames capturing the same motion state share the same phase regardless of which camera records them or when, naturally establishing spatiotemporal correspondence across unsynchronized cameras. We validate Phase-DGS under temporal offsets, frame drops, and camera freezes, achieving up to +8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines while enabling seamless integration with existing DGS backbones including RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS.

2611.04221.tldr: Adds a 1.28M-parameter selective state-space (Mamba) adapter with fixed-size auxiliary memory to frozen CUT3R-style recurrent 3D reconstruction; it lowers trajectory and depth error with periodic resets, with constant memory and throughput up to 2000 frames.
2611.04221.why: It directly targets streaming feed-forward 3D reconstruction (CUT3R/TTT3R) with bounded state and an efficient SSM-based memory, which is relevant to long-sequence 4D reconstruction.
2611.04221.reason: Streaming feed-forward 3D reconstruction with fixed-capacity memory; adjacent to core
2611.04221.qn: Reasonable matched ablations and real-robot tests, but incremental adapter on a narrow baseline set.
2611.04221.abs: Streaming 3D reconstruction must maintain geometric quality over long inputs within a fixed GPU budget. A pretrained recurrent model provides bounded state, but freezing its backbone also fixes its learned state-observation interactions. We introduce Mamba3R, a jointly designed state-memory adapter that provides a trainable adaptation path without updating the backbone or task heads. A selective state-space mixer jointly transforms native state features and a fixed-capacity auxiliary memory, explicit read and write paths carry information across frames, and a decomposed feedback path regulates what the added memory feeds back. Only 1.28 million adapter parameters are trained. Under a shared periodic-reset protocol, it lowers trajectory error and improves accumulated surface and depth accuracy over recurrent baselines on public indoor and outdoor datasets and robot-recorded traversals, gaining up to 40 percent on one metric. Matched comparisons support both the choice of the mixing operator and the utility of carrying the auxiliary memory across frames. Allocated memory remains unchanged and throughput moves by at most 1.4 percent from one to two thousand frames. Replaying its recorded traversals offline, the platform's RTX 4060 averages 11.7 frames per second within 5.1 GiB with the same checkpoint, a mean throughput covering the 10 Hz sensor rate.

2611.04173.tldr: Iterative loop for driving-scene Gaussian Splatting: render novel lateral trajectories, train a new reconstruction on them, re-render original views to get degraded-real pairs that match novel-view artifacts, and retrain the DriveRestorer; adds a soft-planar ground model. Waymo FID drops 15.1% vs ReconDreamer++.
2611.04173.why: It ties video-diffusion restoration to 3DGS reconstruction for novel-trajectory rendering, which is relevant to 4D reconstruction and world-model simulation, though the setting is driving-specific and incremental.
2611.04173.reason: Dynamic 4D driving scene reconstruction with generative priors; close to core 4D reconstruction interests
2611.04173.qn: Sensible self-training loop, but incremental journal extension with modest gains over own prior work.
2611.04173.abs: Dynamic driving scene reconstruction has made remarkable strides in recent years by leveraging generative priors, particularly in the quality of novel trajectory rendering. Nevertheless, a significant gap remains between the generated data and real-world sensor observations, severely hindering further improvements in reconstruction fidelity. In this paper, we present ReconDreamer#, a self-evolving framework that synergizes reconstruction and generation for dynamic driving scenes, which substantially bridges the gap between synthesized novel trajectory data and recorded real-world observations. Within this self-evolving closed-loop framework, the generative and reconstruction models mutually reinforce each other through iterative refinement, ultimately yielding a significant enhancement in the 3D representation capability of the reconstruction model. Additionally, we introduce a geometry-prior-based adaptive ground model to further enhance the rendering quality of the reconstruction model. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks. Specifically on Waymo, at a 6-m lateral shift, ReconDreamer# improves NTA-IoU and NTL-IoU by 8.8% and 3.0%, respectively, and reduces FID by 15.1% relative to ReconDreamer++.

2611.04164.tldr: ReCR is a training-free method for autoregressive video generation that selects a sparse visible context from generated history using decoder representations, then remaps it to a compact causal axis. It improves long-horizon stability across several backbones under matched token budgets.
2611.04164.why: Directly relevant to efficient inference and long-horizon video world models: context selection under a KV budget complements sparse attention and caching, and offers a test-time way to reduce drift.
2611.04164.reason: Autoregressive video decoding with context selection, relevant to video world models
2611.04164.qn: Sensible training-free idea; benchmark gains and 3D consistency evidence appear modest and heuristic.
2611.04164.abs: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.

2611.04416.tldr: FLASH edits images natively at 2K/4K with a frozen 1K full-attention anchor branch plus a high-res branch using local Halo attention, spatial YaRN, and optional progressive 1K-prefix denoising; gets 4.2x faster forward and 30.5% lower progressive latency.

2611.04416.abs: Instruction-based image editors still primarily operate at 1K, whereas practical editing increasingly requires faithful 2K/4K outputs. Dense high-resolution adaptation preserves the editing trajectory but incurs expensive target-source attention; editing at 1K followed by external refinement is cheaper but can separate detail restoration from the editing trajectory. We introduce FLASH, a native high-resolution editor based on sparse cross-resolution denoising. A frozen 1K branch provides a semantic and structural anchor, while a target-resolution branch reconstructs local detail within the same Transformer. An asymmetric topology retains full 1K attention, guides high-resolution queries with spatially aligned low-resolution noisy-target states, and confines high-resolution target-reference interaction to local Halo neighborhoods. Resolution-specific diffusion-state mapping and spatial YaRN adapt the pretrained editor to larger grids. An optional, training-free progressive path replaces early high-resolution denoising with a 1K prefix and completes refinement in the same editor. On VINS-4KEval, the direct model achieves the strongest structural fidelity among the compared methods at both 2K and 4K. A separate 4K forward benchmark with R = 1 records 4.2x faster total forward execution and 25.3x faster attention than dense target-reference attention. Progressive inference reduces end-to-end 4K latency by 30.5%, with a modest quality cost.

2611.04374.tldr: IGSW decomposes dynamic urban Gaussian appearance into weather-shared albedo/normals and weather-specific irradiance/residuals, then gates unreliable diffusion-edited teacher regions; reports better content similarity, semantic consistency and temporal error than baselines on nuScenes and Waymo.

2611.04374.abs: High-fidelity weather editing of 4D scenes can support end-to-end training and closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving. Combining generative image editing with dynamic Gaussian representations enables multi-weather scene reconstruction, but weather-edited images often contain structural distortions. Directly fitting their appearance may propagate errors from teacher images into the reconstructed 4D scene, compromising the original scene structure and temporal continuity. To address these challenges, we propose IGSW, a two-stage framework that combines intrinsic-decoupled 4D Gaussian scene modeling with structure-preserving weather refinement. In Stage I, background Gaussian appearance is decomposed into weather-shared albedo and normals and weather-specific irradiance and residuals. Weather teacher images generated by a diffusion-based image editing model and intrinsic maps estimated by a diffusion-based inverse renderer provide feature-level soft supervision for stable structure and illumination changes. In Stage II, a structure-preservation gate combines semantic conflicts with cross-weather intrinsic discrepancies to suppress unreliable teacher regions. Per-Gaussian weather transport variables and target-weather branches then strengthen the desired weather appearance over the intrinsic-decoupled scene. Experiments on nuScenes and Waymo show that IGSW achieves the highest content similarity and semantic consistency and the lowest temporal error among the compared methods, while retaining pronounced weather-dependent illumination and atmosphere. The project page is available at https://akaxi6.github.io/IGSW/ .

2611.04195.tldr: SettleSplat is a monocular online 3DGS mapping system for scenes where objects move then settle. It lifts 2D DINOv2 uncertainty into per-Gaussian dynamicity for pruning, and gates geometric contradictions by rendered depth uncertainty. It outperforms baselines on Bonn and Co-Fusion.
2611.04195.why: Online 3DGS mapping in dynamic scenes touches your 3D/4D reconstruction interests, but this is a narrow SLAM-style pipeline rather than a video-diffusion or world-model method.

2611.04195.qn: Sensible heuristic pipeline; limited benchmarks and likely hand-tuned components.
2611.04195.abs: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.

2611.02846.tldr: SpecOPD trains parallel speculative-decoding drafters with on-policy distillation by sampling independent draft branches at reference anchors and scoring them via tree masks and state replay, reporting up to 41% longer acceptance length and 16x training throughput.
2611.02846.why: Relevant as an inference-efficiency technique with attention-architecture handling (full, sparse, linear). Speculative decoding ideas could transfer to few-step video diffusion, but this paper targets LLMs.

2611.02846.qn: Broad evaluation across models and attention types; engineering-heavy, incremental over prior OPD work.
2611.02846.abs: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, $16.09\times$ supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to $3.56\times$ generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.

2611.01939.tldr: VLSplat extends codebook-based Gaussian grouping (Unified-Lift) with VLM text-prompted masks and an object scene graph, using intra-group denoising and inter-group candidate acquisition to improve indoor 3D semantic and instance segmentation.

2611.01939.abs: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at https://vlsplat.github.io/.

2611.00177.abs: Egocentric observations provide a robot-centric view of manipulation processes, capturing contact interactions and object-state changes that are important for visuomotor policy learning but difficult to observe from external cameras. However, collecting such data at scale remains expensive due to additional hardware requirements and platform-specific deployment costs. Synthesizing egocentric observations from large-scale exocentric manipulation videos provides a scalable alternative. However, existing methods struggle to synthesize physically consistent and policy-relevant egocentric videos under substantial viewpoint transformations, severe occlusions, complex object interactions, and inherently sparse observations from available exocentric viewpoints.

2611.04055.tldr: HybridSpec adaptively picks the verification length for speculative decoding on GDN-MoE hybrid LLMs, uses a router-boundary correction and block-parallel GDN kernels, reaching 1.30-1.33x speedup over DFlash and 1.75-1.88x over autoregressive decoding.
2611.04055.why: Relevant to efficient inference and linear-attention hybrids, but it targets LLM text decoding, not video diffusion transformers; the draft/verify cost-balancing ideas may loosely transfer.
2611.04055.reason: Speculative decoding for GDN-MoE models; adjacent to efficient inference, not video diffusion.
2611.04055.qn: Solid systems engineering, but narrow: batch-one, greedy decoding, specific hybrid models.
2611.04055.abs: In speculative decoding, parallel drafters such as DFlash make drafting cheap, so target verification dominates each round. A central choice is the verification length, the number of tokens that the target processes in each round. Verifying more draft tokens can accept more of them, but work after the first rejection is wasted. For hybrid target models that combine Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, verification time grows much faster with this length than for dense models. In a single-request profile of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with DFlash, it grew by 71% from length 4 to 16, almost entirely in GDN and MoE layers, compared with 4%-6% for a dense Qwen3-4B target. Each GDN layer must update a recurrent state at every token and recover it at the end of the accepted prefix. The MoE cost depends on the experts that the tokens activate, which are known only once verification runs. We present HybridSpec, which selects the verification length on the GPU from draft-side acceptance estimates and measured target latency. Verification then runs this length plus one extra token up to the first MoE router, before any expert runs. There, a lightweight routing correction uses the observed expert assignments to decide whether to keep that token. The rest of verification runs only on the selected tokens. Block-parallel GDN kernels avoid storing a state after every token and reconstruct the accepted state of every GDN layer in one launch. In isolated benchmarks at verification lengths 4 to 16 with every draft token accepted, these kernels, including accepted-state reconstruction, are $1.54\times$-$4.04\times$ faster than the default kernels. With three GDN-MoE target models in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is $1.75\times$-$1.88\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding and $1.30\times$-$1.33\times$ faster than DFlash.

2611.03768.tldr: MLI lets each DeepSeek Sparse Attention layer use the previous indexer layer's top-k selection, so indexer scans overlap with attention. With no retraining, it decodes up to 14.5% faster than IndexCache at equal retention, with accuracy within a few points.
2611.03768.why: It is sparse-attention inference efficiency for long contexts. The overlap trick and cross-layer selection reuse could carry over to sparse attention in video DiTs, though this paper covers only LLM decoding.
2611.03768.reason: Efficient sparse attention inference; relevant technique but for LLMs not video
2611.03768.qn: Practical, well-evaluated systems trick; gains modest and specific to DSA decode.
2611.03768.abs: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

2611.04479.reason: Structured sparse attention projection; relevant to sparse attention interest
2611.04479.qn: Theoretical sparsity projection with proofs; no transformer experiments visible
2611.04479.abs: In this paper, we introduce the Cone Alignment Index (CAI), a scale-invariant sparsity measure associated with a Lorentz-cone geometry. We provide a probabilistic analysis of the distribution of the CAI score, including a general theorem and explicit corollaries for Gaussian and uniform distributions. As a consequence, we show that, in the high-sparsity regime, the probability that the samples lie within the convex cone tends to one. Building upon this formulation, we derive two complementary projections: the \emph{Parametric Linear Conic Projection} (PLCP), an efficient closed-form approximation, and the \emph{Parametric Euclidean Conic Projection} (PECP), the exact Euclidean projection onto the cone boundary. Our analysis establishes several fundamental theoretical properties. We prove that PLCP and PECP are collinear, differ only by a positive radial scaling factor, and induce exactly the same sparsity threshold, thereby preserving an identical active support. Furthermore, we derive a support-identification theorem showing that, for any prescribed sparsity level $l<n$, the number of coefficients discarded at each iteration is theoretically controlled. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop a bilevel PLCP framework for structured matrix sparsification. The proposed method naturally generates hardware-friendly structured sparsity patterns, including row-wise, column-wise, and diagonal masks, making it particularly well suited for accelerating Transformer attention mechanisms.

2611.04657.reason: Attention pruning via token bias relates to efficient transformer attention
2611.04657.qn: Simple attention pruning idea; evidence limited to classification ViTs
2611.04657.abs: Attention is known to be sparse in vision transformers. In particular, we analyze the unequal relevance of attention-matrix columns to the final computation and show that this phenomenon becomes increasingly pronounced with network depth. This can be interpreted as saying that tokens have an absolute importance for the attention process, independently of queries. Inspired by this, we propose a reformulation of the attention formula that makes this phenomenon explicit by adding an input-dependent bias to the query-key dot product. We show that this new term gives each token a scalar value indicating its anticipated influence on other tokens during the attention process, and can thus serve as a proxy for pruning attention maps. Across multiple transformer model sizes, this allows us to substantially reduce the computational cost of attention, in terms of both FLOPs and inference latency, while retaining most of the original classification accuracy. We publicly released the code and models at https://github.com/EIDOSLAB/AttentionWithBias.

2611.04492.reason: Action-conditioned 3D world model with voxel latents; touches world models
2611.04492.qn: Ambitious 3D world model with multimodal predictions; evidence details limited
2611.04492.abs: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.

2611.05062.reason: Uses video generation backbone and 3D scene flow for robot world models
2611.05062.qn: Interesting 3D motion intermediate idea, but evidence described only qualitatively
2611.05062.abs: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.

2611.04711.reason: World action model using video priors; adjacent to world models
2611.04711.qn: Coupled action-video cycle consistency; benchmark gains on LIBERO-Pro and DROID
2611.04711.abs: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.

2611.04386.reason: Few-step sampling and distillation for text-to-image diffusion; adjacent to efficiency interests
2611.04386.qn: Merges distillation stages for few-step diffusion; compute savings reported
2611.04386.abs: A deployable text-to-image diffusion model must hold several capabilities at once, such as instruction following, text rendering and human preference, and must sample in a few steps. Capabilities and few-step sampling are built in separate stages: a full-step model first consolidates capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation, then serves as a fixed teacher for step distillation. Every full-step model we evaluate scores lower once compressed, and the second stage cannot begin until the first finishes. We introduce StepX-OPD, which merges the two stages: one student acquires every capability while learning to sample in a few steps, so frozen specialists supervise it on the states its own rollout visits rather than on a longer trajectory it never runs. Because a decomposition of the rollout's KL weights velocity mismatch most heavily near the clean end, we also regress the student's velocity on the low-noise part of the rollout. Separately, we find that capability integration makes models write prompt words into images on prompts that never asked for text, and we give a variant that lowers it. We evaluate on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev across instruction following, text rendering, image quality and human preference. On both architectures, StepX-OPD attains the highest normalized average score among the four-step methods compared and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation.

2611.04358.tldr: EndoS3 is a Gaussian Splatting semantic SLAM for endoscopy that uses instance masks to separate static and dynamic instances via camera-compensated flow residuals, gives each instance its own warp field and control nodes, and adds the CRCD++ dataset. It reports beating prior methods.
2611.04358.why: Instance-aware deformable Gaussian SLAM with dynamic/static decomposition relates to 4D reconstruction, but the application is surgical-specific and the techniques are incremental adaptations.

2611.04358.qn: Sensible composition of known components; narrow domain, small ex-vivo benchmark, details unverified.
2611.04358.abs: Purpose: Despite advances in 3D surgical scene understanding, semantic simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM) remains under-explored for two key reasons. First, it requires solving three challenging tasks in parallel: camera pose tracking, high-fidelity deformable reconstruction, and semantic mapping, making progress particularly demanding. Second, the scarcity of datasets providing the necessary ground truth to evaluate all three tasks comprehensively under conditions that closely reflect real surgical procedures environments. Method: We propose EndoS3, a Gaussian Splatting-based semantic SLAM framework that uses instance masks to guide all three tasks. An instance-level motion decomposition module separates static and dynamic instances by evaluating residual flow after compensating for camera motion, accounting for flow noise and comparing motion across neighbouring instances. The camera is tracked against the static Gaussians, while an instance-aware warp field gives each dynamic instance its own control nodes and deformation network. A semantic node allocation module redistributes a fixed node budget across instances according to their size and non-rigidity. We also introduce CRCD++, an ex-vivo Cholecystectomy dataset with RGB-D frames, camera pose and instance annotations for full semantic SLAM evaluation. Results: EndoS3 surpasses all state-of-the-art general-purpose and surgical semantic SLAM methods in tracking, reconstruction and semantic mapping on the CRCD++ and SemSup datasets. Conclusion: Semantic-aware motion and deformation modelling is vital to surgical semantic SLAM. EndoS3 and CRCD++ offer a method and benchmark for improved geometric and semantic understanding in endoscopy.

2611.03043.tldr: VideoEditor-MoE upcycles a 5B video editing DiT into 14B and 56B MoE models with ~8B active parameters, adding routed key–value experts to attention alongside sparse MLPs. It beats MLP-MoE and explicit-guided MoE baselines, and decoupled weight decay stabilizes expert scaling.
2611.03043.why: It is a sparse-capacity scaling study for video DiTs, covering MoE attention, routing behavior across noise levels, and upcycling stability. These are relevant to efficient video transformer design.

2611.03043.qn: Reasonable MoE-attention idea and analyses, but the introduction gives little quantitative evidence.
2611.03043.abs: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.

2611.05361.tldr: A pipeline turns mobile LiDAR, images and poses from localization datasets into per-view depth and visible point-cloud references, using a depth-gap visibility score to tune Hidden Point Removal. It yields ~3x the density of Poisson reconstruction at similar AbsRel, and is used to benchmark feed-forward models against SfM on BotanicGarden.
2611.05361.why: Offers a zero-shot benchmark of feed-forward geometry models (VGGT-style) versus SfM in vegetation; notes duplicated structures in feed-forward reconstructions, a useful failure mode.
2611.05361.reason: Benchmarks feed-forward 3D reconstruction and depth in outdoor scenes
2611.05361.qn: Practical benchmark engineering; limited novelty, LiDAR reference noise and narrow domain.
2611.05361.abs: Reliable evaluation of visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetation-rich outdoor environments is limited by the scarcity of geometric ground-truth data and the cost of complete scanner surveys. We present a LiDARbased reference-generation pipeline for evaluating the zero-shot performance of feed-forward visual-geometry models alongside conventional structure-from-motion (SfM) methods. The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localization datasets to generate per-view depth maps and visible reference point clouds. To address visibility errors in accumulated LiDAR scans, we introduce the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal(HPR). Experiments on TartanAirV2 and TartanGround show that, compared with Poisson surface reconstruction, which is an approach suited to completed scan surveys, the combined HPR and LDGVS filtering retains approximately three times the point density at comparable absolute relative error. We also apply the pipeline to the BotanicGarden dataset to systematically compare depth estimation and 3D reconstruction methods. Feedforward methods produce dense depth predictions efficiently, but their 3D reconstructions can contain duplicated structures. Conventional SfM generally produces more coherent geometry, but its reconstructions remain sparse and more prone to failure in challenging vegetated scenes. The benchmark toolkit and datasets will be released.
